transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Derek (Redwood SE), Priya (Lead ML Eng - Acme), Marcus (Platform Eng - Acme), Hannah (Security - Acme), Oliver (PM - Acme)

Summary:
- Integration/discovery call focused on how Acme would integrate Redwood APIs into their existing stack (Python/Node services, LangChain/LlamaIndex experimentation) and options for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments. Security, rate limits, and observability hooks were key concerns. Next: send SDK examples, schedule technical deep dive for private deployment and run a small benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, this is Sofia from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with me is Derek our solutions engineer. How are you folks doing?
[00:08] Priya: Good thanks, morning everyone. We were hoping to go through integration patterns and understand what changes we need to make to our gateway/proxy.
[00:15] Derek: Great. Quick agenda: integration options (SDKs + direct REST), LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy considerations (rate limiting, retries), observability hooks (webhooks, traces, metrics), and deployment modes (hosted, dedicated, private). We'll also talk about quotas and throttles.
[00:30] Marcus: Quick context — our stack is primarily Python microservices, some Node for front-end APIs, we run an env in AWS (VPC), use Kong as an API gateway today. We're evaluating for a customer-facing assistant so latency is important but so is cost.
[00:45] Derek: Understood. On SDKs, we have official Python and Node SDKs, small footprint. For teams using LangChain or LlamaIndex, we provide example connectors — basically you can swap in Redwood as the LLM provider with minimal code changes. The example notebooks demonstrate prompt templates, streaming, and tooling for embeddings.
[01:05] Priya: When you say "swap in", does that handle tokenization differences or do we need to re-tokenize locally?
[01:10] Derek: Good question. Tokenization is model-specific. Our SDK does not re-tokenize, it sends the prompt to the model. We provide a token-usage estimator in the SDK to help you understand cost impact; for benchmarking we recommend running a local tokenization pass with the same tokenizer as the model you pick (we can share tokenizer binaries or point to HF tokenizers).
[01:28] Hannah: From security side, we need details on VPC/private deployment, KMS integration, and audit logs. Also SSO/SCIM for RBAC — how does Redwood support that?
[01:36] Sofia: For Private deployments we offer a customer-controlled control plane running in your VPC or on-prem. KMS/HSM integrations are supported (bring-your-own-key) and we surface audit logs. For Hosted we offer enterprise options with dedicated tenancy and encryption-at-rest with customer-managed keys as an add-on. We also support SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning for enterprise accounts.
[01:55] Oliver: If we choose Dedicated vs Private, what's the delta operationally?
[02:00] Derek: Dedicated is Redwood-managed reserved capacity in our infra but logically isolated — predictability in throughput and SLA. Private is customer-controlled network and often required for strict compliance: control plane runs in your VPC and you manage networking. For Dedicated you get predictable qps and lower ops burden; Private gives you the most control but it needs more involvement from your infra team.
[02:20] Marcus: We're curious about the gateway — can we route requests through our Kong instance and still get the observability hooks?
[02:26] Derek: Yes. Two common patterns: 1) Proxy all calls through your gateway to Redwood's REST endpoints — you keep rate-limiting, auth, and logging upstream. 2) Use our SDK inside services and let Redwood's ingest hooks (webhooks/traces) forward observability back to your systems. We provide OpenTelemetry-compatible traces and token-level cost metrics via the Console. If you proxy, ensure you pass headers for request-id and auth, and configure timeouts for streaming responses.
[02:50] Priya: About rate limits and quotas — we expect bursts up to ~250 qps for the assistant; average 50 qps, median response length 120 tokens. What are the options to avoid tail latency spikes?
[03:05] Derek: For Hosted, you can start with our standard quota and apply burst policies: you can set rate-limits per API key and per-route. We also offer reserved Dedicated pools for guaranteed throughput which mitigate tail spikes. Caching prefixes and KV cache for session state reduces per-token compute. We also recommend batching where appropriate and streaming to lower perceived latency.
[03:26] Priya: Do you expose metrics we can scrape? We want per-request latency breakdown into network/queue/compute.
[03:33] Derek: Yes, Redwood Console surfaces token-level latency breakdowns and we export Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, and per-route dashboards. You can also push logs to your SIEM; for Private we can forward logs into your logging stack directly.
[03:48] Hannah: Any constraints when using LangChain or LlamaIndex — will function calling or streaming be supported?
[03:55] Derek: We support streaming and function/tool calling. LangChain might need small adapter code — our sample adapters handle stream iterators and function calls. For LlamaIndex, we provide an indexer example that writes embeddings to your vector store (or our managed embeddings storage) and uses Redwood for generation. We do see occasional hiccups with third-party libs around streaming edge cases, we'll include robust examples.
[04:17] Priya: We use a custom LLM gateway for A/B routing between models. Can Redwood be a backend for that?
[04:23] Derek: Absolutely. You can treat Redwood as a model backend behind your gateway. We also support smart routing inside Redwood (by policy) if you prefer Redwood to handle model fallbacks and region routing, but many customers run their own routing layer and call Redwood endpoints as one of several targets.
[04:38] Marcus: On observability hooks — do you provide request ids or headers we should correlate?
[04:43] Derek: We return a Redwood-request-id header on responses, and recommend passing your own x-request-id header. Our SDK attaches tracing metadata automatically if you pass a tracer. The Console exposes token-level breakdowns and you can map request-ids to traces.
[04:56] Oliver: On pricing, are embeddings charged differently? We have a vector search pipeline.
[05:00] Sofia: Yes, embeddings and generation calls are priced separately. We'll send the pricing deck, but embedding unit cost is lower and we have volume discounts and reserved capacity pricing for Dedicated. Also note that caching and deduping can significantly reduce embedding spend.
[05:14] Priya: For the pilot we want to run both a hosted and a dedicated benchmark — can Redwood help run a 48-hour benchmark with sample traffic?
[05:21] Derek: Yes, we typically run a benchmark: provide us your prompt set and traffic profile, we spin up a dedicated pool for the test if you want to test Dedicated, or we can run hosted under your account with increased quotas. We'll measure p95/p99 latency, token cost, and quality regressions.
[05:38] Hannah: Security follow-ups — we need SOC 2, encryption details, data retention options, and a contact for legal/infosec.
[05:45] Sofia: I'll send the security deck and a redacted SOC 2 report. We have configurable retention, and for Private you can set retention via your storage policies. I'll include our security contact in the email.
[05:56] Oliver: Any integration pitfalls you've seen with Kong or other gateways we should be mindful of?
[06:01] Derek: Timeouts and streaming handling — Kong/NGINX by default can buffer streaming bodies; you need to turn buffering off for server-sent events/streaming endpoints. Also ensure you forward response trailers and chunked encodings. Auth header propagation and rate-limit headers are the other common hiccups.
[06:20] Priya: We also evaluate using LlamaIndex for retrieval-augmented generation, we currently have a Redis vector store. Does Redwood have any connectors or do you expect us to route embeddings?
[06:30] Derek: We have examples for common vector stores (Redis, Pinecone), and you can either push embeddings to your store or use Redwood's managed embeddings storage. LlamaIndex adapter will show how to write to Redis and then call Redwood for generation with retrieved context.
[06:45] Priya: Are there SDK examples for streaming responses into a web socket or SSE?
[06:50] Derek: Yes, our Node SDK has an example for SSE and websockets, and Python asyncio examples. We'll include those in the repo we send.
[06:58] Marcus: On quotas — if someone hits the quota at the gateway, what's the recommended retry/backoff? Do you provide headers to indicate remaining quota?
[07:06] Derek: We return standard rate-limit headers (x-rw-rate-limit-remaining, x-rw-rate-limit-reset). For retries, exponential backoff with jitter is recommended; for idempotency you should use request ids. For streaming calls, we recommend client-side timeouts + graceful fallback to a shorter response.
[07:25] Sofia: Okay wrapping up — let me recap next steps. Derek will send LangChain/LlamaIndex examples and a benchmark script; I'll send pricing and the security pack; Acme will share prompts and workload profile; we'll schedule an SE deep dive for Private deployment. Anything to add?
[07:39] Priya: That's correct. One ask — include sample tokenization scripts so we can estimate cost before the benchmark.
[07:45] Derek: Will do. Also I'll include a short Kong configuration checklist for streaming.
[07:51] Hannah: Please include the legal contact and any standard DPA templates you have.
[07:55] Sofia: Yep, we'll include that. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the artifacts and proposed times for the deep dive.
[08:02] Priya: Thanks all. Bye.
